In summary, our research is concerned with

a possible ecological impact of a Bt transgenic potato cultivar that has been engineered to express a toxin specific to the Colorado potato beetles, on a polyphagous insect pest, Spodoptera littloralis.
a potential ecological risk of genetically modified potatoes to nontarget insects.
the impact of the Cry3Aa toxin, expressed in a potato cultivar, on a non-target insect, S. littoralisa moth that feeds on the leaves of potato.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the expression of Cry3A toxin in the potato cultivar NewLeaf Superior has a deleterious impact on the polyphagus moth S. littorali.
the Cry3Aa toxin, expressed in potato, reduces the fecundity of a polyphagous pest insect.
Cry3Aa is not a specific insect toxin and that it should not be used to control polyphagous insects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a genetically modified crop cultivar that is designed to be resistant to a particular insect species may have an unexpected negative impact on another insect species that is a potential crop pest.
the Cry3Aa protein, which was designed to control a major insect pest of potato in the United States, may also affect a major pest of tomato in the same country and other countries.
the Cry3Aa toxin, which was designed for use against a beetle, also has a deleterious impact on a moth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of Cry3A toxins for the protection of potato plants against L. decemlineata is associated with an increased risk to S. littoralia, a moth species that is a pest of a variety of crops.
the use of a Bt protein in genetically modified plants that is toxic to non-target species should be avoided.
the use of Bt toxins to confer resistance to a pest species can affect other insect species that share the same habitat.
